stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 4 hours of central chest pain. His ECG shows no ST-segment elevation. At 6 hours after symptom onset, high-sensitivity troponin I is elevated, while CK-MB remains normal. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
stemHtml: A 58-year-old man presents with 4 hours of central chest pain. His ECG shows no ST-segment elevation. At 6 hours after symptom onset, high-sensitivity troponin I is elevated, while CK-MB remains normal. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis? (Question Id: 502123)
keywords: “ECG shows no ST-segment elevation” – Rules out STEMI, points toward NSTEMI or unstable angina.
“High-sensitivity troponin I is elevated” – Confirms myocardial injury; distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina.
keywordsHtml:
1. “ECG shows no ST-segment elevation” – Rules out STEMI, points toward NSTEMI or unstable angina.
  2. “High-sensitivity troponin I is elevated” – Confirms myocardial injury; distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina.

B.title: Confirms NSTEMI
B.body:
NSTEMI is diagnosed when there is myocardial injury evidenced by elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin) without ST-segment elevation on ECG.
This patient has elevated high-sensitivity troponin I at 6 hours, CK-MB normal, and no ST-elevation, which fits NSTEMI criteria.
Key point: Troponin is more sensitive than CK-MB and rises earlier in myocardial injury. NSTEMI can be diagnosed even if CK-MB is normal.
B.bodyHtml:
• NSTEMI is diagnosed when there is myocardial injury evidenced by elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin) without ST-segment elevation on ECG.
  • This patient has elevated high-sensitivity troponin I at 6 hours, CK-MB normal, and no ST-elevation, which fits NSTEMI criteria.
  • Key point: Troponin is more sensitive than CK-MB and rises earlier in myocardial injury. NSTEMI can be diagnosed even if CK-MB is normal.

A.title: Confirms STEMI
A.body:
STEMI requires ST-segment elevation on ECG or new LBBB.
In this patient, ECG is normal, so STEMI is not present.
A.bodyHtml:
• STEMI requires ST-segment elevation on ECG or new LBBB.
  • In this patient, ECG is normal, so STEMI is not present.

C.title: Suggests unstable angina
C.body:
Unstable angina presents with chest pain at rest or new-onset, normal ECG or nonspecific changes, and no rise in cardiac biomarkers.
This patient has elevated troponin, so UA is excluded.
C.bodyHtml:
• Unstable angina presents with chest pain at rest or new-onset, normal ECG or nonspecific changes, and no rise in cardiac biomarkers.
  • This patient has elevated troponin, so UA is excluded.

D.title: Indicates pericarditis
D.body:
Pericarditis often presents with diffuse ST-elevation, PR depression, and chest pain that changes with posture.
Biomarkers may be mildly elevated but usually not isolated troponin rise without ECG changes.
D.bodyHtml:
• Pericarditis often presents with diffuse ST-elevation, PR depression, and chest pain that changes with posture.
  • Biomarkers may be mildly elevated but usually not isolated troponin rise without ECG changes.

E.title: Excludes ACS
E.body: Elevated troponin confirms myocardial injury, so ACS cannot be excluded.
E.bodyHtml: • Elevated troponin confirms myocardial injury, so ACS cannot be excluded.

keyConcept: NSTEMI is diagnosed in patients with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin) without ST-segment elevation. High-sensitivity troponin is more sensitive than CK-MB. Unstable angina occurs with normal biomarkers, and STEMI requires ECG changes.
keyConceptHtml: NSTEMI is diagnosed in patients with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin) without ST-segment elevation. High-sensitivity troponin is more sensitive than CK-MB. Unstable angina occurs with normal biomarkers, and STEMI requires ECG changes.

metadata.subtopic: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) - STEMI vs NSTEMI (Pathophysiology & Biomarkers)

cells: Definition
Myocardial ischemia with elevated cardiac biomarkers but no ST-segment elevation on ECG
Differentiates NSTEMI from STEMI and unstable angina
cellsHtml: Myocardial ischemia with elevated cardiac biomarkers but no ST-segment elevation on ECG
Differentiates NSTEMI from STEMI and unstable angina

cells: Symptoms

Central chest pain,
often at rest or minimal exertion,
may radiate to arm/jaw/back,
associated with sweating,
nausea
Guides initial clinical suspicion
cellsHtml:
• Central chest pain,
  • often at rest or minimal exertion,
  • may radiate to arm/jaw/back,
  • associated with sweating,
  • nausea

cells: ECG Findings

Normal or nonspecific ST/T changes,
no ST elevation
Helps rule out STEMI
cellsHtml:
• Normal or nonspecific ST/T changes,
  • no ST elevation

cells: Biomarkers

High-sensitivity troponin I/T elevated,
CK-MB may be normal or mildly raised
Confirms myocardial injury
cellsHtml:
• High-sensitivity troponin I/T elevated,
  • CK-MB may be normal or mildly raised

cells: Risk Factors

Hypertension,
diabetes,
smoking,
dyslipidemia,
older age,
male sex
Important for prevention and prognosis
Management

Antiplatelets (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor),
anticoagulants,
beta-blockers,
statins,
early invasive strategy if high risk
Reduces morbidity and mortality
cellsHtml:
• Antiplatelets (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor),
  • anticoagulants,
  • beta-blockers,
  • statins,
  • early invasive strategy if high risk

cells: Complications

Heart failure,
arrhythmias,
recurrent ischemia,
cardiogenic shock
Requires monitoring and timely intervention
Unstable Angina
Chest pain at rest or minimal exertion
No elevation of cardiac biomarkers; ECG may show ST depression or T-wave inversion
cellsHtml: Chest pain at rest or minimal exertion
No elevation of cardiac biomarkers; ECG may show ST depression or T-wave inversion

cells: STEMI
Chest pain with ST-segment elevation on ECG
ECG shows ST elevation, usually higher troponin rise
cellsHtml: Chest pain with ST-segment elevation on ECG
ECG shows ST elevation, usually higher troponin rise

cells: Myocarditis
Chest pain, viral prodrome, sometimes fever
Troponin elevated, ECG may show diffuse ST changes; cardiac MRI may help
cellsHtml: Troponin elevated, ECG may show diffuse ST changes; cardiac MRI may help

cells: Pericarditis
Sharp chest pain, relieved by leaning forward
ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and PR depression, biomarkers may be mildly raised
cellsHtml: Sharp chest pain, relieved by leaning forward
ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and PR depression, biomarkers may be mildly raised

cells: Pulmonary Embolism
Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia
Troponin may rise, ECG may show S1Q3T3 pattern, imaging confirms PE
cellsHtml: Troponin may rise, ECG may show S1Q3T3 pattern, imaging confirms PE

cells: Aortic Dissection
Sudden severe tearing chest/back pain, pulse deficit
Troponin may rise; CT angiography shows dissection
cellsHtml: Sudden severe tearing chest/back pain, pulse deficit
Troponin may rise; CT angiography shows dissection

cells: Severe Heart Failure / Tachyarrhythmias
Dyspnea, edema, palpitations
Troponin may rise due to demand ischemia; ECG and echo help differentiate
cellsHtml: Troponin may rise due to demand ischemia; ECG and echo help differentiate

diagram.heading: Acute Coronary Syndrome NSTEMI (Non–ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction)
diagram.description: This diagram illustrates the pathophysiology of NSTEMI, showing partial coronary artery occlusion leading to subendocardial ischemia and myocardial necrosis. It highlights key clinical features, ECG findings (no ST elevation with possible ST depression/T-wave inversion), and the role of elevated troponin in diagnosis, along with an overview of initial management strategies.
